On-Policy Distillation — Kevin Lu and colleagues, Thinking Machines Lab (2025)

A year ago, Thinking Machines described a simple recipe: let a small model write its own answer, and have a stronger model score every word of it. Jack and Molly unpack "On-Policy Distillation" (Kevin Lu and colleagues, October 2025): how it combines the word-by-word signal of imitation with reinforcement learning's habit of training on the student's own attempts; its lineage from Hinton, Vinyals and Dean's 2015 soft targets through Google DeepMind's and MiniLLM's 2023 papers and Qwen3; and how DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5 and NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Ultra now use it to fold RL-trained teachers into one model. Then the twist: Anthropic and OpenAI accuse Chinese labs of distilling their models, and the emerging legal line, in a White House memo and two bills, turns on authorization rather than technique.

Notes: the post's nine-to-thirty-times compute saving is its own estimate against an extrapolated fine-tuning baseline that was never run; Qwen's firmer head-to-head (74.4 vs 67.6 on AIME 2024 at about a tenth of the GPU hours of RL) is one 8-billion-parameter model on math and code questions, run by Qwen's team. What the accusations describe, copying outputs and using a model as a grader, is the same family of technique but not the post's method, since closed APIs don't score text another model wrote. The accusations are allegations, and the accused have not answered on the record as far as reporting shows. Neither bill is law (the House bill cleared committee 43–0); the critique of its terms-of-service prong is Molly's own reading.

Jack and Molly are AI-generated hosts; research and script by Oggy.
